newsitem.title: CANADA: Beleaguered Canadian defense minister resigns.
newsitem.headline: Beleaguered Canadian defense minister resigns.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien dismissed his beleaguered defense minister, David Collenette, on Friday for having inappropriately interfered with an immigration case.
But Chretien said he hoped to bring his long-time friend and political ally back into his cabinet.

The two main opposition parties, the Bloc Quebecois and the Reform Party, had demanded Collenette resign in connection with an alleged cover-up of an incident during a peacekeeping mission several years ago in which Canadian soldiers tortured and killed several Somalis.

But Collenette told a news conference that his official resignation had nothing to do with Somalia and solely with having breached guidelines by having written a letter asking for swift action on an immigration case.
"It's the only honorable thing to do," said a sombre Collenette, a long-time political ally of Chretien.
Collenette was the third cabinet minister in Chretien's three-year tenure to leave office in controversy.
Deputy Prime Minister Sheila Copps resigned in May from the cabinet and Parliament over a broken tax promise but was brought back into cabinet after winning a special election.
In January Chretien pushed aside another much-criticized official, Canadian Heritage Minister Michel Dupuy, who had written on behalf of a constituent to the agency that regulates broadcasters.
Chretien had won a landslide election in 1993 from the Conservatives, partly because of voter frustration with scandals under former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney.
Chretien said he was extremely sorry to accept Collenette's resignation but added: "I told him that I hope soon I'll be in a position to take him back into my cabinet."

"I think it's very kind of him to offer to bring me back into cabinet but there are no guarantees in politics. I appreciate what he said but that's all," Collenette said, adding he would stay in Parliament and seek re-election.

The Bloc Quebecois' deputy leader, Suzanne Tremblay, said she was suspicious of the circumstances of the resignation: "I think this smells like a false pretext. Mr. Colennette will be back in cabinet after a few months."
The resignation came about as the result of a request from a private citizen under Canada's Access to Information law.
Collenette said it came to the attention of Chretien's chief of staff, Jean Pelletier, that the letter he wrote in March to the Immigration and Refugee Board was about to be released.

"I have...been informed that this letter breached the draft guidelines which you have provided to ministers concerning communications between members of the cabinet and quasi-judicial bodies," Collenette wrote Chretien.

Collenette was replaced by Human Resources Development Minister Douglas Young. Minister of International Cooperation Pierre Pettigrew replaced Young, and the Liberal whip in the House of Commons, Don Boudria, replaced Pettigrew.
Although the Somalia incident occurred during the Canadian peacekeeping mission in 1992-1993, before Collenette took office, he was criticized for susequent actions.

He drew heavy fire in recent months for having backed Chief of Defense Staff General Jean Boyle after Boyle admitted breaking the spirt of Canada's freedom of information laws. Boyle, meanwhile, remains Canada's top soldier.
